As for your question, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years. The earliest recorded observations of the night sky date back to ancient civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece around 4000-5000 years ago. These early cultures believed that the sky was a dome above the Earth, and that the stars and planets were gods or spirits.

The idea that space was a void of darkness, illuminated only by stars and galaxies, developed over time through the work of ancient Greek philosophers such as Aristotle and Epicurus. They proposed that the universe was infinite in size and that the stars and planets were separate from the Earth.

However, it wasn't until the 16th century that the concept of a vast, empty space beyond the Earth's atmosphere began to take shape. The Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus proposed a heliocentric model of the universe, where the Sun was at the center and the planets orbited around it. This idea was later developed by Galileo Galilei and Johannes Kepler, who observed the motion of the planets and developed the laws of planetary motion.

The modern understanding of outer space as a vast, dark void was further developed in the 19th and 20th centuries through the work of astronomers such as William Herschel, Friedrich Bessel, and Edwin Hubble. Hubble's observations of the universe in the 1920s and 1930s revealed the existence of galaxies beyond the Milky Way, and the expansion of the universe itself.

As for the idea that space was blue like the morning sky, this is a misconception that has been debunked by scientists. The color of space is actually black, as it absorbs all wavelengths of light. The stars and galaxies we see in the night sky appear white or blue because they emit light of all wavelengths, but the space itself is not blue.

It's worth noting that the idea of a blue sky in space may have originated from the fact that the Earth's atmosphere scatters shorter wavelengths of light, such as blue and violet, more than longer wavelengths, such as red and orange. This is why the sky appears blue during the day on Earth. However, in space, there is no atmosphere to scatter light, so the sky appears black.
